entries.title: Props to Pelley for speaking out after '60 Minutes' firing
entries.summary: <p>Respect and appreciation to Scott Pelley — who was recently fired from <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/06/04/60-minutes-chaos-after-bari-weiss-fired-scott-pelley/" target="_blank" >“60 Minutes”</a> by CBS News — for<a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DZIKsSwmbHf/" target="_blank" > boldly expressing</a> truth to power, standing up for the most essential First Amendment rights and fighting those who would diminish them.</p><p>How many today have the gumption to say what's right, as Pelley did in his public statement following his firing? How many have the gumption to DO what's right?</p><p><i>Maria Sklavounou, West Ridge</i></p><h3>Language matters when discussing city’s youth</h3><p>Thank you for publishing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/06/03/teen-takeovers-public-spaces-downtown-youth-disinvestment-online-culture-almethia-franklin" >opinion piece</a> by Almethia C. Franklin in last week's Sun-Times. I wish everyone would read it, particularly those who express outrage about what they — we — call "teen takeovers."</p><p>Franklin points out that language can construct social realities and shape public policies that develop from the starting viewpoint that Black youth are invading a space where they do not belong. Many in city government have approached these gatherings as a menace to society and have mostly offered punitive methods to suppress and eliminate them.</p><p>Franklin's point that social media is being used to connect individuals from historically warring factions of the city sheds a light of optimism in a bleak time. Social media often functions as a tool to bring young people together in the same physical space — not isolate them.</p><p>Many city leaders have given lip service to the idea that more must be done to offer young people spaces and opportunities. But they start from the assumption that the mostly Black youth do not have the same right as others to be anywhere in the city. That is neither fair nor helpful.</p><p><i>Rebecca Wolfram, Lawndale</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-520000" name="module-520000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Tornado, storm preparedness </h3><p>I am a Boy Scout from Lemont. I am currently working on my <a class="Link" href="https://www.scouting.org/merit-badges/communication/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=scouting.org-programs-meritbadges&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=10640049575&gbraid=0AAAAACT4EJ_ZfWzH6QifAQjKESU2EbwFy&gclid=CjwKCAjwxITRBhBYEiwA6mZm7UjwWbGfzl5fKsWGHeaS9HbhbkEEpfTLm4RUyXAAFl4BotXYLf4KBRoC7X8QAvD_BwE" target="_blank" >Communication Merit Badge</a>. Since we are still in <a class="Link" href="https://stateclimatologist.isws.illinois.edu/climate-of-illinois/tornadoes-in-illinois/" target="_blank" >tornado season in Illinois</a>, I wanted to share my ideas about storm preparedness.</p><p>Severe storms and tornadoes affect many people across the United States every year. Our country should do more to help people stay safe and prepared before storms happen.</p><p>More people should take tornado sirens seriously and pay attention to emergency alerts. These warnings can help protect people during dangerous weather. I also think magazines, newspapers and online media should teach more tornado safety, so the public knows what to do in an emergency.</p><p>People should also keep their wireless emergency alerts on so they can get important weather warnings on their cellphones.More people should join <a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/skywarn/" target="_blank" >Skywarn</a>, a volunteer program that trains people to report severe weather to the National Weather Service.</p><p>Another idea would be to create an advertisement campaign that shares a storm preparedness checklist. Some important items people should know about or keep on hand could include:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-d1230631-6036-11f1-8de3-ff396e336916" start="1"><li>National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Weather Radio</li><li>Fully charged cellphones with emergency alerts turned on</li><li>A wallet and emergency money</li><li>Shoes</li><li>Medications</li><li>Flashlight</li><li>First aid kit</li><li>Safe shelter location</li><li>Anything else your family feels is important</li></ol><p>Being prepared before a storm can help keep people safe when severe weather happens.</p><p><i>Vinny Genovese, Lemont</i></p><h3>Trump excels at hiring most unqualified</h3><p>I heard a news report about people being surprised by the appointment of <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/06/03/politics/bill-pulte-trump-cabinet-picks-experience" target="_blank" >Bill Pulte</a>, who has no obvious qualification to succeed Tulsi Gabbard, the previous record holder for lack of qualification, for director of national intelligence</p><p>I was surprised that anybody was surprised. Where have these people been for the last 16 months? During this time, Donald J. Trump has put an endless parade of people whose qualifications stretch no farther than the willingness to do his dirty work into positions of high importance, thus exposing the citizens of the United States to various risks. The appointment of Pulte was no surprise to me at all.</p><p>I have concluded that many of the things Trump has done seem more coherent if my base assumption is he has been "hired" by those who tasked him with undermining the U.S. and disrupting the world order that has served us well for three-quarters of a century.</p><p><i>Curt Fredrikson, Mokena</i></p><h3>Expanding health care access is imperative</h3><p>Access to affordable, high quality health care is not a luxury — it is a basic necessity that affects every person in this country.</p><p>Yet millions of Americans continue to struggle with rising medical costs, limited access to primary care and insurance gaps that leave families one illness away from financial crisis. These challenges are especially prevalent in low‑income neighborhoods, rural communities and among people living with chronic conditions.</p><p>Chicago is no exception. Too many residents delay care because they cannot afford a doctor’s visit. Others travel miles outside their communities just to find a primary care provider accepting new patients. These barriers don’t just harm individuals — they weaken the health of our entire city.</p><p>That is why legislation like the <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3385" target="_blank" >Lower Health Care Costs Act</a> deserves serious attention. The bill aims to reduce medical expenses, increase transparency and expand access to affordable care. But passing a bill is only part of the solution.</p><p>We need a health care system that prioritizes patients over profit, strengthens primary care and ensures no one is denied treatment because of their income or ZIP code. That means investing in community clinics, expanding telehealth, improving insurance affordability and holding large health care corporations accountable for price hikes that burden families.</p><p>Chicagoans deserve a system that works for them — not one that forces them to choose between paying rent and filling a prescription. Addressing these issues is not just good policy. It is a moral responsibility.</p><p><i>Joei Langford, Pullman</i></p><h3>Changing our tune</h3><p>If the Bears move to Hammond, what will become of the fight song, "Bear Down. Chicago Bears?" It wouldn't make sense to sing "You're the pride and joy of Illinois!"</p><p><i>Michael Shawgo, Edgewater</i></p>

entries.title: 'Make no little plans': A lesson for Trump
entries.summary: <p>One thing we know about Donald Trump: He has no patience with little plans.</p><p>“Most people think small,” he wrote in "Art of the Deal" with co-author Tony Schwartz, “because most people are afraid of success, afraid of making decisions, afraid of winning.”</p><p>Trump also wrote: “I like thinking big. I always have. To me it's very simple: If you're going to be thinking anyway, you might as well think big.”</p><p>Arguably, Trump’s approach to just about everything hangs on four personal convictions: Create (and broadcast) your own reality; always show toughness; never back down; and — perhaps most importantly — always go big.</p><p>Well, maybe. Nothing wrong with pursuing big ideas, but perhaps Trump could learn a thing or two from looking at the example of one of Chicago’s premier architects and city planners of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, <a class="Link" href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Daniel-Burnham" target="_blank" >Daniel Burnham</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5a0000" name="module-5a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Burnham's big thinking transformed the built environment of our city and reshaped land and cityscapes across the country and around the world, from the National Mall in Washington to a summer capital in the <a class="Link" href="https://burnhamplan100.lib.uchicago.edu/events/id/1403/ " target="_blank" >Philippines</a>.</p><p>In fact, it was Burnham who first, and most memorably, gave us the credo that has inspired Trumpian big thinkers everywhere. “<a class="Link" href="http://www.encyclopedia.chicagohistory.org/pages/2396.html" target="_blank" >Make no little plans</a>,” he’s reported to have said. “They have no magic to stir men’s blood.”</p><p>He said this in the context of his Plan of Chicago, the landmark document that represented one of the earliest attempts to make comprehensive city planning — with lots of bulldozing and demolishing and rebuilding and reshaping — an accepted part of governance in the modern American city.</p><h3>Many grand plans ‘will not be realized’</h3><p>So Trump could easily look to Burnham as a kindred spirit in the realm of making big things happen, full speed ahead.</p><p>But not so fast. What else does Burnham say right after his most famous quote? He says many of those grand not-so-little plans “probably themselves will not be realized.”</p><p>What? But Mr. Burnham, if the plans won’t be realized, why make them?</p><p>It turns out that Burnham had plenty of modesty and restraint in his clarion call for thinking big. It’s just that for over 100 years people didn’t fully understand what he meant by making “no little plans.”</p><p>For a long time, scholars struggled to find a definitive source for the statement. In the 1950s, Henry H. Saylor, an eminent editor of architectural publications, even wrote an academic journal article titled “ ’Make No Little Plans’: Daniel Burnham Thought It, But Did He Say It?”</p><p>The conclusion? Maybe he said it, but who knows where and in what context? The most likely source was a speech given in London in 1910, but in the official transcript, “make no little plans” was nowhere to be seen.</p><p>Then, in 2019, Chicago tour guide and history buff <a class="Link" href="https://mysteriouschicago.com/finding-daniel-burnhams-no-little-plans-quote/" target="_blank" >Adam Selzer</a> found a transcription of several key segments of the speech in a 1910 issue of the Chicago Record-Herald<i>. </i>The piece was<i> </i>titled “Stirred by Burnham, Democracy Champion.” And, sure enough, Burnham did say the famous phrase. And more.</p><h3>Think big, seek agreement</h3><p>As the headline indicates, the speech itself was not just about refusing to settle for little plans; it was about making significant change in a <i>democracy, </i>specifically — in city planner Burnham’s case — how to actively reimagine “a city of the future under a Democratic government.” The only way to do it? Actively seek agreement and public buy-in. Emphasize the “demos<i>”</i> in democracy.</p><p>Once Burnham’s big plans were crystallized in the Plan of Chicago, he knew many parts of the plan would lie dormant for years, decades or longer. But there they would be, waiting to be reawakened and reinvigorated when the time might be right and the public felt the need or the benefit. He wasn’t in a hurry. He would take what he could get.</p><p>And the results were impressive. After Burnham’s death in 1912, his friends and associates managed to accomplish a great deal with public support — building the DuSable Bridge, widening and extending North Michigan Avenue into today’s Magnificent Mile, building the double-decker Wacker Drive, expanding and refining green spaces around the city, to name just a few.</p><p>To this day, many parts of the plan remain undone, incomplete, replaced or forever out of the mix.</p><p>The lesson for Trump? Take the wins. Listen to stakeholders. Seek public support, patiently and deliberately. Absorb the losses, comforting yourself with the possibility that, if your plans really are good and beneficial, they may be revived long after you have vanished from the scene. Make no little plans, sure, but make good ones — democratically — that the public will actually embrace, now or in the future.</p><p><i>Trygve Thoreson is an emeritus professor of English and humanities at Harper College in Palatine. He is the author of the recently published book "Daniel Burnham and Louis Sullivan: Personal Histories of Two Icons of American Architecture."</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8c0000" name="module-8c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Libertyville tight end Brock Williams commits to Texas
entries.summary: <p>How good is Brock Williams?</p><p>Good enough for a national power to venture well away from its usual recruiting base to reel him in.</p><p>The Libertyville tight end committed to Texas on the Pat McAfee Show last month, adding the consensus No. 79 player in the country to coach Steve Sarkisian's 2027 class.</p><p>"It says a lot for a team like Texas coming up to get him," national recruiting analyst Clint Cosgrove told the Sun-Times. "You don't see them dipping into Illinois often."</p><p>But it makes sense for the nation's elite programs to be chasing Williams. A 6-foot-5, 230-pounder, he's the No. 5 player in the state in the 2027 recruiting cycle and the No. 4 tight end.</p><p>Williams emerged on recruiters' radar as a sophomore in 2024 when he was one of the top targets for Wildcats quarterback Quinn Schambow, who threw for 3,521 yards and 52 touchdowns that season. Williams had 35 catches for 608 yards and seven TDs in 2024 before pulling in 44 passes for 596 yards and 11 touchdowns last fall.</p><p>Showing his versatility, Williams also returned punts and kickoffs, averaging 24.8 yards per runback. And he even completed his only pass attempt for 32 yards.</p><p>"He is so natural with his ball skills," Cosgrove said. "He reminds me of (former South Elgin standout and Miami recruit) Gavin Mueller a lot.</p><p>"After the catch, he plays nasty. He's a physical kid."</p><p>Williams had almost 40 offers, including pretty much every college football blue blood: Alabama, Georgia, Indiana, LSU. Miami, Michigan, Ohio State and Notre Dame, among others.</p><p>"The recruiting process over the past few months has been insane," Williams said on the McAfee show.</p><p>But he felt confident in his choice.</p><p>"You can't go wrong with coach Sark, especially his offense he's putting you in," Williams said on the broadcast. "You're going to have top-of-the-line quarterbacks, the best quarterbacks in the country. So that's huge for me as well."</p><p>Cosgrove expects Williams to fit in well in the Longhorns' offensive scheme.</p><p>"Even if it's contested, he catches the ball," Cosgrove said.</p><p>Cosgrove described one notable reception that displayed Williams' situational awareness: "He had to turn around and catch it. There were people behind him. He made the perfect cut and took it for a touchdown."</p><p>Not every player, even every good one, can handle the spotlight of playing in Austin.</p><p>"It's always a big culture shock when a kid goes from the Midwest to the University of Texas," Cosgrove said.</p><p>But Williams has the skills and the makeup to make that leap.</p><p>"I think he's got a chance to be a weapon," Cosgrove said.</p><p><b>Lake Zurich hires Teonic</b></p><p>Former Hersey,, Larkin and South Elgin coach Dragan Teonic has been hired at Lake Zurich.</p><p>He replaces Ron Planz, who stepped down after leading the Bears to a 51-24 record over seven seasons. Planz's teams twice advanced to the semifinals and had two other trips to the quarterfinals.</p>

entries.title: Boy, 13, charged with wounding 4 other kids in mass shooting on Chicago's South Side
entries.summary: <p>A 13-year-old boy was charged Monday with shooting four other children over the weekend in the Grand Boulevard neighborhood on the South Side.</p><p>The teen allegedly pulled out a gun around 9:40 p.m. Saturday in the 4500 block of South Prairie Avenue and opened fire on the other boys, according to Chicago police. Responding officers later found the four boys suffering from gunshot wounds.</p><p>An 11-year-old boy was struck in the leg and a 13-year-old boy was shot in the foot, police said. They were both taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition.</p><p>Another 13-year-old boy suffered a gunshot wound to the leg and was taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition, police said. A 14-year-old was grazed in the back and taken to Comer in fair condition.</p><p>The boy charged in the attack was arrested about 20 minutes later in the 4600 block of South Calumet Avenue, according to police. He was charged with felony counts of aggravated battery, unlawful possession of a weapon and having a gun without a valid license to own one.</p><p>He was expected to appear at a detention hearing Monday in juvenile court, police said.</p>

entries.title: Funeral services announced for Spencer Leak Jr.
entries.summary: <p>Funeral services have been announced for Spencer Leak Jr., one of the leaders of the Chicago funeral titan Leak and Sons. </p><p>Leak’s public visitation will take place Thursday from 4-8 p.m. at Leak and Sons Funeral Home, 7838 S. Cottage Grove Ave., the funeral home confirmed. A celebration of life will be held June 13 at 10 a.m. at the House of Hope, 752 E. 114th St.</p><p>Leak, one of three sons of Spencer Leak Sr., <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/05/31/spencer-leak-jr-sons-funeral-homes-dies" target="_blank" >helped run the family funeral homes</a> for more than 45 years as they grew and remained a staple of the South Side’s Black community.</p><p>The family has handled the funerals of several notable Chicagoans through the years, including soul singer Sam Cooke, comedian Bernie Mac, rapper Juice WRLD and drug kingpin William Morris “Flukey” Stokes. Earlier this year, they hosted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/02/26/leak-sons-funeral-home-jesse-jackson-services-rainbow-push-history-civil-rights-leader" target="_blank" ><u>the Rev. Jesse Jackson Sr.’s funeral</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: High school basketball summer storylines to watch
entries.summary: <p>With June's summer shootouts upon us, which includes two “live” period weekends where college coaches will be out evaluating prospects, the high school basketball calendar has officially turned the page to 2026-27.</p><p>High school coaches will get to start molding their teams for a few weeks this month through team camps, shootouts and summer leagues.</p><p>Here are a four questions to be answered in the coming weeks.</p><p><b>Where will the players land?</b></p><p>While always prevalent to some degree over the many decades of high school basketball, transfers are at an all-time high. Transfers have become a way of life and the norm in the sport.</p><p>There are two times of the year to keep an eye on player movement. The first is the arrival of June basketball as players register at new schools and teams assemble for the aforementioned “live” events. The other is when school officially begins in August.</p><p>Many players have already departed their school for others. But the expectation is several of the state’s best will be on the move sooner than later, significantly altering a power shift or absence in the sport.</p><p><b>Who’s No. 1?</b></p><p>There isn’t an obvious preseason No. 1 team heading into 2026-27, though the early contender is Neuqua Valley.</p><p>The return of the high-scoring duo of Cole Kelly, one of the top 50 prospects in the Class of 2028, and Illinois commit Mason Martin is elite. It’s not every day you return two high-major prospects who scored 40-plus points a night a year ago.</p><p>In addition to Kelly and Martin, there are several experienced pieces returning for coach Todd Sutton. How good that supporting cast develops and improves in the offseason, which we will get a glimpse of in June, could determine the viability of Neuqua Valley in the top spot.</p><p><b>Who’s the best prospect in 2028?</b></p><p>There are two highly-ranked national prospects in the junior class: Kelly and Bolingbrook’s Brady Pettigrew.</p><p>Both are enjoying stellar offseasons that have led to high-profile camps and tryouts, recognition and all kinds of high-major interest.</p><p>The national rankings will tell you Pettigrew has the edge. He’s ranked as high as No. 13 in the country by ESPN and is a consensus top 20 player in the country. And while the 6-3 guard is the No. 1 ranked prospect in the state, the gap is closer than some realize</p><p>But we’ll take what seems to be a high level but pretty friendly and respectful competition between the two standouts.</p><p><b>What new names will emerge?</b></p><p>The names of up-and-coming freshmen are introduced during the season. Some take the opportunity by storm while others dip their toe in the deep end while gaining valuable experience.</p><p>All of it is a lead up to blossoming as sophomores. So what players in the Class of 2029 are poised to emerge and set the stage this summer for a big sophomore season?</p><p>Keep an eye on the Mount Carmel duo of DK Heard and Ronald Johnson, who showed glimpses a year ago. Big man Elon Henderson of Leo and Young’s TJ Jamison did as well and are set to make a jump.</p><p>Bloom guard Keiwon Gulley and New Trier’s 6-7 Denym Wallace produced as freshmen, while St. Laurence’s Evan Lemons and Payton’s Orlando Bohlen are flying under the radar.</p><p>But look for the biggest jumps and impact from a pair of players outside the Chicago area: Emaurion Jackson of East St. Louis and Dallas Marshall of Bloomington. These two are loaded with talent and feature attractive measurables as big, long perimeter players.</p>

Huh/AP Photos file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whhkjyd-l-k/" target="_blank" >Bears’ board of directors votes to push stadium to Hammond, Indiana</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whhkjyd-l-u/" target="_blank" >Patrick Finley</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whhkjyd-l-o/" target="_blank" >Fran Spielman</a></h5><p><b>Bear Down south?</b>: The Bears’ board of directors met Thursday and decided to move forward with their plans to build a stadium in Indiana, positioning the team to play its home games out of state for the first time in its 106-year history. The team announced Friday it would "advance our stadium development project in Hammond."</p><p><b>Illinois still an option</b>: The Bears' Friday announcement tips the scales significantly toward Indiana — but falls short of eliminating Illinois from contention. A source said <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whhkjyd-l-b/" target="_blank" >Arlington Heights is still an option</a>, if the state finds a way to give the Bears property tax certainty on the 326-acre plot they own. It’s unclear if waiting until the Senate and House reconvene this fall would be too late, though. The team considers Arlington Heights — not Chicago — the only viable choice in Cook County.</p><p><b>Dome dreams</b>: The Bears were lured by a sweetheart deal approved by Indiana three months ago, when lawmakers there authorized a stadium authority backed by taxes on admissions, hotels, restaurants and tolls. The Bears have committed $2 billion to their stadium project. The team would keep all revenue generated by the stadium and have the option to buy it back in 40 years, when Indiana taxpayers have paid off the bonds.</p><p><b>What's next</b>: The Bears <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whhkjyd-l-n/" target="_blank" >have a lot of work to do on the Hammond site before they can finalize a deal</a> — dozens, if not hundreds, of boxes to check in Indiana, ranging from big-picture finalizing details to the mundane traffic studies. entries.title: Over 100 ex-federal prosecutors call out 'failure of leadership' by Chicago's embattled U.S. attorney
entries.summary: <p>More than 100 former federal prosecutors who served in Chicago and Rockford delivered an extraordinary rebuke of U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros on Monday, concluding there’s been a “failure of leadership”<b> </b>in an office with “a renowned history of excellence pursuing justice.”</p><p>The 111 signatories include individuals identifying as Democrats, Republicans and independents — all now acting as private citizens. They pointed to an exodus of leadership from Boutros’ office, grand jury irregularities, an unusual number of collapsed cases and a breach of trust with judges.</p><p>“These matters raise questions about whether there is a failure of leadership in the office we deeply respect and whether once-forbidden political considerations are infecting prosecutorial decisions,” they wrote. “The answer to both questions, in our view, is yes.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/03/26/chicago-trump-justice-department-doj-webb-lassar-fitzgerald" >Ex-federal prosecutors in Chicago taking on Trump’s ‘troubling’ DOJ: ‘We feel compelled to speak and act’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It’s the latest in a string of highly unusual developments following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >the collapse of the so-called “Broadview Six” case</a> over apparent prosecutorial misconduct during grand jury proceedings. Boutros’ office<b> </b>initially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >secured a conspiracy indictment</a><b> </b>against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters, but the case was later pared down<b> </b>to misdemeanor charges against four of them.</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/06/04/trump-blanche-boutros-doj-broadview" target="_blank" >a statement<b> </b>last week</a>, Boutros accused unnamed individuals of having “capitalized on the opportunity to attempt to destabilize the office, distract us from our mission, and wreak discord among our once-united [federal prosecutor] and law enforcement community under the guise that they love or even really care about this incredible and storied office.”</p><p>Now, the two statements combined seem to reveal a level of tension not seen in recent memory between Chicago’s top federal prosecutor — who leads the U.S. attorney’s office — and the community of former prosecutors who once served there.</p><p>It’s all part of the continued fallout from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2025/09/09/trump-midway-blitz-ice-justice-department-chicago-bears-soybean" target="_blank" >Midway Blitz</a>, the unprecedented Trump administration deportation campaign that pummeled Chicago last fall. Former Attorney General Pam Bondi <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >appointed Boutros to his job</a> on a temporary basis<b> </b>in April 2025. The following summer, Chicago’s federal judges picked Boutros to continue in the role on a more permanent basis.</p><p>“For decades, our former office earned a reputation for winning significant cases while playing by the rules,” the former prosecutors wrote Monday. “We hope that the next few months will provide an opportunity to begin an effort to restore this reputation. That, however, will require candor from U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros; the courage to stand above and apart from political fealty; and a willingness to address the failures that have occurred.</p><p>“It will require action, not mere words.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-100000" name="image-100000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e4f582/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/746a0b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/717494e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Dirksen Federal Courthouse, 219 S. Dearborn St. | Rich Hein/Sun-Times" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/717494e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d724b75/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/717494e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4104x2303+0+213/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F9e%2F05fe8f1f50a8ade928c7c1c11c09%2Fdirksen-02.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Dirksen Federal Courthouse at 219 S. Dearborn St. in Chicago’s Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Rich Hein/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>They began their statement by quoting U.S. District Judge April Perry, who presides over the “Broadview Six” case. A former federal prosecutor in Chicago herself, she told Boutros’ team May 21 that, “your sole goal is to do justice. Your client is justice itself.”</p><p>The statement goes on to identify four areas of concern,<b> </b>starting with “the departure of many senior, experienced leaders and prosecutors in the office.” Most department heads have left since Boutros arrived.</p><p>“Turnover always occurs,” the former prosecutors wrote, “but the volume of veteran prosecutors leaving the office over the last year is extraordinary. The challenge is exacerbated by the hiring of new [federal prosecutors] who require time to fully grow into their jobs but will be without an abundance of valuable mentors.”</p><p>Boutros has said that “some people left because I told them I was going to demote them. Some people left because they came into my office and they said that they strongly dislike this administration and cannot work for this administration.”</p><p>Second, the former prosecutors pointed to Boutros’ appearance before the grand jury panel that handed up the indictment against the “Broadview Six” later that same day.<b> </b>Boutros released his remarks to the grand jurors in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/02/durbin-duckworth-boutros-broadview-ice-trump" target="_blank" >an unusual special report</a> last week.</p><p>Boutros told panel members they are the “conscience of the community”<b> </b>and encouraged them to listen to the evidence. He also said, “if there’s anyone here who is struggling with a certain type of cases, such as the immigration cases or other cases … I would ask that you raise your hand.”</p><p>The former prosecutors called that an "extraordinary step”<b> </b>— noting that Boutros’ request that grand jurors raise their hand came after the panel had already once rejected the “Broadview Six” case.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/02/durbin-duckworth-boutros-broadview-ice-trump" >Chicago’s top federal prosecutor details unusual briefing of grand jury ahead of ‘Broadview Six’ indictment</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“The message he delivered effectively signaled that the head of the U.S. Attorney’s Office is unhappy with us and we did something wrong,” the former prosecutors wrote. “That message is inappropriate.”</p><p>Next, the group pointed to the poor conviction rate for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >prosecutions tied to Midway Blitz</a>. Of 33 known defendants in such cases, only two have pleaded guilty. Twenty-four people have been cleared, and five others have struck deals putting their charges on track for dismissal.</p><p>Grand jurors rejected criminal charges against at least three of those defendants. That’s in addition to their initial rejection of the “Broadview Six” case.</p><p>“The pattern and timing of charging decisions, public rhetoric surrounding the operation, and the extraordinary collapse rate of these prosecutions raise at least the appearance that improper considerations supplanted the office's historical exercise of prosecutorial discretion free from political influence,” the former prosecutors wrote.</p><p>Boutros has said the office’s traditional protocols didn’t work because<b> </b>“we were dealing with an out-of-town group” of hundreds of law enforcement agents in an unprecedented situation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Finally, the former prosecutors pointed to a breach of trust with judges. It’s a likely reference to the apparent effort to redact misconduct out of grand jury transcripts given to Perry by the feds. The judge told Boutros’ team last month that<b> </b>“trust has been broken.”</p><p>“When judges increasingly call into question the motivation or candor of prosecutors and agents, that is a sure sign the standard has been compromised,” the former prosecutors wrote.<b> </b>“The abuse of trust is devastating and reversing that tide must be a top priority of the office’s leadership.”</p>
entries.author: Jon Seidel

entries.title: Policía de Chicago cierra investigación de accidente durante un arresto caótico de ICE en Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>La Policía de Chicago cerró rápidamente una investigación sobre un accidente de choque y fuga que involucró a un agente federal de inmigración mientras detenía a un hombre la semana pasada en Albany Park, según informó el Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>El accidente ocurrió el martes por la mañana en la cuadra 3100 al oeste de Lawrence Avenue, donde agentes de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/03/agentes-de-ice-paralizan-a-un-hombre-con-taser-y-embisten-su-auto-en-un-arresto-caotico-en-albany-park" target="_blank" >persiguieron, electrocutaron y detuvieron</a> a un hombre sin camiseta mientras una multitud se agrupaba y documentaba el violento arresto. Antes de que el hombre fuera aprehendido, un agente de ICE pareció chocar contra el auto de una mujer.</p><p>La Policía de Chicago respondió a la escena, entrevistó al conductor y a un testigo, y tomó informes después de que los agentes se habían ido. En un reporte de policía, indicaron que un agente de ICE realizaba un “movimiento táctico” en el momento del choque y que el incidente fue clasificado como "no criminal".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b40000" name="module-b40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Un portavoz de la policía dijo que la investigación fue suspendida porque no había “más pistas investigativas adicionales”, aunque videos y fotos tomados por un reportero del Sun-Times y otros transeúntes captaron el choque y partes de la detención.</p><p>El viernes, un agente de seguros que gestiona el reclamo de la mujer dijo que no había recibido respuesta del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) ni de los federales, señalando que ICE le dio “la vuelta” en varias llamadas.</p><p>"No quieren tener nada que ver con esto”, dijo el agente de seguros. “Sabemos quién es el culpable aquí. Lo tenemos en video, así que esto debería ser más rápido. CPD tiene video de esto”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ysQNeEB3ecE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="ICE agents shock man with Taser, barrel into car during chaotic arrest in Albany Park"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Las tácticas usadas durante la detención recordaron las que se vieron durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportación de la administración de Trump que generó miles de arrestos en el área de Chicago el otoño pasado.</p><p>Aunque los arrestos han disminuido desde entonces y se han vuelto más focalizados, los defensores de los inmigrantes y los voluntarios han <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/08/equipos-de-respuesta-rapida-de-chicago-cambian-tacticas-ante-baja-visibilidad-de-control-migratorio" target="_blank" >seguido rastreando la actividad de ICE</a> en Chicago y en los suburbios. Desde el inicio de este año hasta mediados de marzo, 580 personas habían sido detenidas en el área<u>,</u> según un análisis de registros realizado por Sun-Times/WBEZ del Proyecto de Datos de Deportación.</p><p>A principios de este año, una comisión encabezada por el gobernador JB Pritzker culminó con un informe que instaba a la Policía de Chicago, a la oficina de la fiscal del estado del Condado de Cook y a otras agencias a investigar y procesar delitos presuntamente derivados del Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>La Policía Estatal de Illinois abrió de inmediato<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/06/policia-del-estado-de-illinois-inicia-investigacion-sobre-tiroteo-mortal-de-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-por-ice" target="_blank" >una investigación</a>sobre la muerte de Silverio VillegasGonzález, quien fue baleado y asesinado por un agente de ICE en el suburbio de Franklin Park enseptiembre. Un juez del Condado de Cook luego rechazó un esfuerzo para <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/26/jueza-del-condado-de-cook-rechaza-nombrar-fiscal-especial-para-investigar-agentes-de-operativo-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >designar a un fiscal especial</a> en la oficina de la fiscal del estado para apuntar a los agentes federales, determinando que las agencias policiales deben remitir casos a los fiscales para que estos puedan presentar cargos.</p><p><b>Una detención impactante </b></p><p>El incidente del martes comenzó a las 8:07 a.m., cuando una Nissan Pathfinder conducida por un agente de ICE giró hacia el este en Lawrence Avenue de Kedzie Avenue, persiguiendo al hombre. Una segunda Pathfinder que transportaba a más agentes salió de un estacionamiento cercano y golpeó el auto de la mujer en un aparente intento de bloquear al hombre para que no escapara.</p><p>Las autoridades federales identificaron al hombre como Domer Jesús Martínez Sifontes, un venezolano que ingresó al país en 2023 y que no tiene estatus legal.</p><p>Los agentes derribaron a Martínez Sifontes al suelo mientras él gritaba pidiendo ayuda, y uno de ellos lo electrocutó con una pistola Taser tras apuntar a los transeúntes. Durante el forcejeo, un agente dejó caer un cartucho de balas, que más tarde fue recogido por un colega.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> amenazaron con arrestar a la mujer cuyo auto había sido golpeado. Docenas de personas se reunieron en la escena, soplando silbatos y gritando a los agentes federales.</p><p>ICE y el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) no respondieron a preguntas sobre el choque, el uso de la fuerza o el cartucho de balas que fue dejado en la calle.</p><p>En un comunicado, DHS afirmó que Martínez Sifontes "agredió a los oficiales e intentó evadir el arresto huyendo a pie", y que luego "continuó resistiendo el arresto" una vez que fue detenido.</p><p>DHS no indicó si Martínez Sifontes tiene antecedentes penales y no parece que haya sido acusado de ningún delito en el Condado de Cook. Permanecerá bajo custodia de ICE mientras se lleven a cabo los procedimientos de deportación.</p><p>Los agentes federales describieron a los residentes que se reunieron en la escena como "agitadores anti ICE", diciendo que uno pintó un vehículo federal y "golpeó un poste de luz".</p><p>"Por su seguridad, los oficiales de ICE abandonaron rápidamente la escena", dijo DHS.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Kankakee basketball star Lincoln Williams picks Illinois
entries.summary: <p>The recruiting timeline for one of the state’s top basketball prospects may have been unorthodox, but it sure made the final days of his high school years memorable.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2025/11/13/kankakee-high-school-basketball-lincoln-williams" >Lincoln Williams</a>, who has been the top uncommitted prospect in the state for months, graduated from Kankakee on May 21. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2025/03/07/chicago-sun-times-all-area-boys-basketball-team-2025" >All-Area</a> guard followed it up with a commitment to Illinois on Monday.</p><p>“I chose to stay home,” said Williams of choosing Illinois over his other two finalists of Virginia Tech and UNLV. “There is a bond I have with the assistant coaches and coach [Brad] Underwood, so I decided to stay home.”</p><p>As the weeks passed following a 29-2 season at Kankakee this past year, Williams kept hearing the question of where he was headed for college. It’s rare for a player who is arguably the top prospect in the class to be uncommitted following his graduation date. But there were self-inflicted obstacles that slowed the process and that he had to overcome.</p><p>“I don’t think a lot of people know, but I struggled with my grades my junior year,” Williams said. “I picked up all those offers my junior year, but then I got a little big-headed, missed some classes a little bit, and struggled with my grades.”</p><p>Williams was close to choosing a school early in his senior year. But each time a school saw the questionable grades from his junior year, the recruiting skid to a halt.</p><p>Williams then put together a big year — not just on the court but in the classroom as well. He recorded all As and Bs throughout his senior year.</p><p>“I know a lot of people were waiting on my decision,” Williams said. “I know they were wondering why isn’t he committing? When is he going to commit? But I was waiting for my final grade report.”</p><p>With his grades intact and commitment made, he now joins an Illinois recruiting class that includes five other incoming freshmen.</p><p>Kankakee coach Chris Pickett has watched Williams develop into an all-around player and says his former star will go down as “the most celebrated Kankakee player to date.”</p><p>“Lincoln’s development and production is a direct result of him being dedicated to the program, the school and the town,” Pickett said. “He wanted to show people that you don’t have to leave to develop and be challenged.”</p><p>The comfort and familiarity with Illinois — and Champaign being just 75 miles south of Kankakee on I-57 — were important factors for Williams in his decision-making. He’s very close with his family. With his mother passing away when he was just a 1-year-old, which is one of the reasons he wears the No. 1 jersey, the family has leaned on one another.</p><p>“It’s always been my dad, brother and sister — always us four being there for each other, being loyal to each other,” Williams said. “Without my mother, that’s how I grew up. Plus my sister went to Illinois for four years before she finished up at Notre Dame, so I was always around there as a kid.</p><p>“But it feels pretty good to be an hour away from where I grew up here in Kankakee. My support system is big and important to me, so I know my family is going to make every game.”</p><p>While Williams was highly productive in his career at Kankakee — he finished as the school’s all-time leading scorer with 1,853 points and put up 26 points a game as a senior — it’s always been about his upside. Everything Williams does as a player is seen through the lens of the physical attributes he possesses as a prospect.</p><p>As a long and rangy 6-6 wing with athleticism and perimeter skills, Williams passes the look test. He plays well in transition and is a threat for lobs and putbacks. And he brings the positional size and versatility Illinois has recently coveted.</p><p>His combination of size, lateral mobility, length and instincts lead you to believe he has the traits to develop into an ultra-disruptive defender in time. Williams already impacts with blocks, steals and deflections while playing the part of a Swiss-Army Knife.</p><p>In addition to adding weight and strength that should come naturally in time, what will ultimately lift him to another level will be the development of his jumper.</p><p>“I am going to go play in the toughest conference in the country,” Williams said of playing in the Big Ten, “so I have work to do. But I can’t wait to get to campus and get to work.”</p>

entries.title: Surprising White Sox could have multiple All-Stars in the offing
entries.summary: <p>PHILADELPHIA — Somebody had to represent the lowly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> in All-Star Games during the depths of the rebuild.</p><p>That’s no knock on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/07/06/shane-smith-all-star-white-sox-rule-5-rookie" target="_blank" ><u>Shane Smith</u></a>, Garrett Crochet or Luis Robert Jr., who each had admirable enough showings to earn their way to Midsummer Classics in the Sox’ string of three consecutive triple-digit-loss seasons.</p><p>But with the team finally showing hints of sustainable competitiveness, nearly half of manager Will Venable’s regular position players are legitimately worthy of All-Star consideration.</p><p>After leaving Philadelphia with a series loss on Sunday, a few Sox players could make their way back to Citizens Bank Park for the July 14 spectacle, which would mark the first time the Sox have sent multiple All-Stars since Tim Anderson and Liam Hendriks earned nods in 2022.</p><p>“We’ve got a number of guys who I hope are in those conversations and I hope are getting the attention that they deserve,” manager Will Venable said, pointing to his squad’s top tier of talent that has spoken for itself.</p><p>Look no farther than injured rookie sensation <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/30/white-sox-place-munetaka-murakami-on-injured-list-call-up-jacob-gonzalez" target="_blank" ><u>Munetaka Murakami</u></a>, whose strained hamstring is expected to heal up sometime around the All-Star Game. His 20 home runs were still good for second in the American League behind Yordan Alvarez after a week on the shelf.</p><p>Murakami’s regular moonshots have stolen some of the spotlight from his teammate across the diamond, Miguel Vargas, whose 15 dingers lead all MLB third basemen, and whose .242/.370/.489 breakout otherwise would be the story of the season. </p><p>Vargas is vying to become the first Sox All-Star at third since Joe Crede in 2008, and potentially the first Sox starter at the position since Jimmy Dykes in 1933.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/18/munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-miguel-vargas-white-sox-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>third “M”</u></a> at the heart of the Sox’ batting order, Colson Montgomery, broke out of a funk in Philly with his 16th homer of the season, extending his lead among MLB shortstops.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div His 2.61 ERA was fourth-best in the American League entering the week, and his eight wins were second-most.</p><p>Versatile, flame-throwing reliever Grant Taylor (1-0, 1.93 ERA) burnished his national profile further over the weekend, mowing down the Phillies with three straight K’s to seal Saturday’s victory. He’s fanned 50 in 32⅔ innings.</p><p>“He's one of the best arms in baseball,” Sox pitching director Brian Bannister said. “One of the better arms I've ever worked with. He's already put up over one WAR on the relief side [1.4 per FanGraphs as of Sunday]. He's as productive as a lot of starting pitchers out there in his role. It just goes to show how dominant he is.”</p><p>And don’t sleep on second baseman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/06/chase-meidroth-white-sox-power" target="_blank" ><u>Chase Meidroth</u></a>, who’s bringing a 19-game on-base streak into Tuesday’s series opener against the Braves, with .735 OPS sitting third at his position across baseball.</p><p>But the biggest surprise inserting himself into the All-Star conversation is Tristan Peters, the Manitoba-born, onetime SIU Saluki and line-dancing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/02/white-sox-savannah-bananas-tristan-peters" target="_blank" ><u>Savannah Banana</u></a> whom the Sox got for peanuts in the offseason. All he’s done is post an .813 OPS while playing a dazzling center field over 62 games that have left fans shaking their heads over the aches and disappointment of the Robert Era.</p><p>“I didn't know much about him, to be honest,” Venable said of the 26-year-old rookie who clawed his way onto the roster in spring training. “He's obviously been a really pleasant surprise, a guy that really works hard, puts himself in a good position to take good swings on good pitches, and obviously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/12/white-sox-tristan-peters-rays-southern-illinois-pete-crow-armstrong-jump-outfielders-statcast" target="_blank" ><u>the defensive part of his game</u></a> speaks for itself.</p><p>“It feels like he hits a double every single day,” Venable said of Peters, who hit four over the weekend and leads MLB center fielders with 15 on the year. “It's really cool to see Tristan take advantage of an opportunity, and he’s been huge for us. He’s been amazing.”</p><p>All-Star voting is open online through June 25.</p><p></p><h3><b>ON DECK</b></h3><p><b>BRAVES AT SOX</b></p><p><b>Tuesday:</b> Grant Holmes (4-2, 3.86 ERA) vs. Erick Fedde entries.title: Evanston Township High School pauses summer classes after weekend cyberattack
entries.summary: <p>Evanston Township High School is closed until at least Wednesday because of a cyberattack that occurred over the weekend, school officials announced. </p><p>A ransomware attack "disrupted access to district systems, internet services and computer infrastructure" and forced the school to cancel summer classes, sports camps and other on-campus activities that were scheduled, according to a note on the high school's website. </p><p>In a statement, the school said closing was necessary because it impacted systems critical to "safely" operating campus, such as network access, internet services, phone services, and other emergency or operational systems."</p><p>ETHS said it didn't yet know when it would reopen, but would determine that within the next 24 hours based on "the progress of the investigation, system restoration, and confirmation that ETHS can safely resume operations."</p><p>"The district is working with cybersecurity forensic experts to determine what information, if any, may have been accessed or acquired," the school said in a statement to the Sun-Times. "Without these systems fully operational, we cannot safely run school or other on-campus activities. Staff are working remotely to the extent they are able, given these limitations."</p><p>The school did "not yet know the full scope of what data may have been impacted" or how it happened, though it was discovered by the school's IT team, it said in a statement. School phone systems aren’t available, and families may not be able to access certain online tools, accounts or school resources, the note said.</p><p>The FBI is looking into the incident, according to the school. The bureau hasn't responded to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: Niegan entrada a Estados Unidos a fotógrafo de la Copa Mundial y un jugador es interrogado en O'Hare
entries.summary: <p>La Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) le negó el ingreso el viernes a un fotógrafo de la selección nacional de fútbol de Irak y mantuvo a un jugador bajo interrogatorio durante horas en el Aeropuerto Internacional O'Hare, mientras el equipo llegaba para un partido de exhibición que se realizará esta semana, en preparación para la Copa Mundial de la FIFA.</p><p>Ambos fueron apartados para una "inspección adicional" después de que la selección nacional de Irak voló desde el Aeropuerto Internacional de Dubái. Las inspecciones son "una parte rutinaria del proceso de inspección de CBP cuando los oficiales necesitan verificar información o determinar la admisibilidad", indicó un portavoz de aduanas.</p><p>Irak se enfrenta a Venezuela en un partido amistoso el martes en el Estadio SeatGeek de Bridgeview. Su primer partido de la Copa Mundial es el 16 de junio en Massachusetts.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0e0000" name="module-0e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Al fotógrafo de la selección nacional de Irak le negaron su ingreso debido a "preocupaciones de evaluación", según el portavoz de aduanas. No se proporcionaron más detalles.</p><p>"Todos los viajeros que buscan ingresar a los Estados Unidos, incluidos atletas, entrenadores y personal, están sujetos a la inspección y evaluación de la CBP. Las determinaciones sobre la admisibilidad se realizan caso por caso, utilizando información de las fuerzas del orden, la seguridad nacional y la inmigración disponible al momento de la inspección", dijo el portavoz de aduanas en un comunicado.</p><p>Según informaron los medios, el jugador detenido para interrogatorio es el delantero de Irak, Aymen Hussein. Reuters informó que estuvo detenido durante casi siete horas.</p><p>La selección nacional de fútbol de Irak ha sido una historia de superación al clasificar para la Copa Mundial de este año, convirtiéndose en el último equipo en hacerlo. Es la primera vez en 40 años que se clasifica para la Copa Mundial, siendo esta su única aparición anterior.</p><p>La Asociación de Fútbol de Irak no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Portillo’s to open Michigan Avenue restaurant
entries.summary: <p>The iconic Chicago-area hot dog chain Portillo’s will open a restaurant on Michigan Avenue, south of the Chicago River.</p><p>The Oak Brook-based company didn’t give an opening date for the location at 304 N. Michigan Ave. But the news marks renewed focus on Portillo’s home market, where the brand renowned for Chicago-style hot dogs and Italian beef sandwiches has a loyal following. It was founded in 1963 as a hot dog trailer in Villa Park and has grown to a national chain.</p><p>“Chicago is where the Portillo’s story began, and opening in the heart of the city is not only an incredibly proud moment for our brand, but also a recognition of how important Chicagoans are, not only to our history, but to our future,” Portillo's CEO <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/restaurants/2026/02/12/portillos-brett-patterson-ceo" target="_blank" >Brett Patterson</a> said in a Friday news release.</p><p>The Michigan Avenue location will be the fourth Portillo’s restaurant in Chicago and the 45th in the Chicago area. The opening will give a boost to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2026/04/16/chicago-loop-alliance-suzet-mckinney-ceo" target="_blank" >the Loop</a>, which has struggled with retail and commercial vacancies after the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>The 5,500-square-foot restaurant will have nearly 100 seats and offer dine-in and takeout, the company said. It’s one of Portillo’s smaller format restaurants that is part of a strategic reset the company announced last fall.</p><p>After private equity firm Berkshire Partners bought Portillo’s in 2014 and the company went public in 2021, Portillo's accelerated nationwide expansion. It has more than 100 restaurants in 11 states including Texas, Georgia, Arizona and Florida.</p><p>But business has flagged and former CEO <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2025/09/23/portillos-ceo-michael-osanloo-resigns-immediately" target="_blank" >Michael Osanloo</a> resigned in September after seven years at the helm. Patterson was named CEO in February. Portillo’s has acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/02/24/portillos-slowing-national-expansion-weaker-sales" >challenges</a> with gaining traction in new territory.</p><p>Revenue for fiscal year 2025, ended Dec. 28, rose 3% year-over-year to $732.1 million, due primarily to recent restaurant openings. But same-restaurant sales, or those open for at least 24 months, fell 0.5%. Net income was $21.1 million, compared to more than $35 million in 2024.</p><p>In fourth quarter 2025, revenue was $185.7 million, compared to $184.6 million the previous year. Net income fell more than 49% to nearly $6.3 million, compared to $12.4 million in fourth quarter 2024.</p>

entries.title: Michael Jordan recalls 'special years' with Stacey King during Bulls' first three-peat
entries.summary: <p>Michael Jordan said Monday he's "deeply saddened" by the death of former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> teammate Stacey King, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/06/07/bulls-announce-former-broadcaster-player-stacey-king-died" >who died Sunday </a>at 59. </p><p>Jordan emphasized King's role on his first three NBA championship teams with the Bulls (1991-93). King was the No. 6 overall pick in the 1989 NBA draft by Chicago and played eight seasons in the NBA before a long career as a beloved color commentator on Bulls' television broadcasts.</p><p>"I'm deeply saddened to learn of Stacey's passing," Jordan said, according to ESPN 1000. "We shared some special years together as teammates, and he was part of a group that helped define an era of Chicago Bulls basketball."</p><p>After his playing and coaching career, King moved to the broadcast booth in 2006, working as a studio analyst for Bulls pregame and postgame shows. He started filling in as a third broadcaster in games late in 2006 and moved to that role permanently in 2007.</p><p><i>Read more at </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com" target="_blank" ><i>usatoday.com</i></a></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/06/07/bulls-announce-former-broadcaster-player-stacey-king-died" >Former Bulls player and broadcaster Stacey King dies at 59</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/07/jason-benetti-cubs-stacey-king-dead-bulls-white-sox-adam-amin-chicago-michael-jordan-scottie-pippen-matthew-boyd" >Jason Benetti, in town to call Cubs, remembers working in ‘partnership’ with Stacey King</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/06/07/chicago-bulls-stacey-king-dead-analyst-tv-broadcast-mark-schanowski-gimme-the-hotsauce-nba-oklahoma" >Quick to turn a phrase, Stacey King entertained, informed on Bulls broadcasts</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: ComEd ofrece hasta $500 a pequeños negocios para pagar sus facturas de luz cada vez más altas
entries.summary: <p>ComEd está ofreciendo pagos de hasta $500 a sus clientes propietarios de pequeños negocios que están navegando para pagar sus facturas de electricidad tras dos años de aumentos de precios relacionados con el crecimiento de los centros de datos.</p><p>Las solicitudes de la subvención estarán disponibles a partir del 15 de junio y se asignarán por orden de llegada. Para más información, visita <a class="Link" href="http://www.comed.com/SMBrelief" target="_blank" >www.comed.com/SMBrelief</a>.</p><p>Se espera que los propietarios paguen una parte del monto como requisito de “cofinanciamiento” de la solicitud de subvención. Así que si debes $1,000, puedes solicitar $500, pero también deberás pagar a ComEd los otros $500.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-510000" name="module-510000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los pagos forman parte de un programa de asistencia de $2.5 millones que la empresa de servicios públicos consideró necesario, ya que los residentes y negocios enfrentan facturas eléctricas más altas, en gran parte debido a la demanda de energía de enormes centros de datos de inteligencia artificial (AI).</p><p>El programa sigue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/06/17/comed-ofrece-pagos-de-500-a-clientes-que-no-pueden-pagar-sus-facturas-de-luz" target="_blank" >un plan similar para clientes residenciales</a> anunciado hace un año.</p><p>“Nuestro enfoque el año pasado fue el residencial y pensamos que el segmento adecuado para centrarnos ahora son los negocios pequeños y medianos”, dijo Gil Quiniones, director ejecutivo de ComEd, en una entrevista.</p><p>Quiniones mencionó que la empresa seguirá trabajando con los negocios en prácticas de eficiencia energética, las cuales, comentó, pueden reducir significativamente las facturas de electricidad.</p><p>Si bien este año no habrá un programa de subvenciones similar para clientes individuales, Quiniones señaló que los residentes cuentan con algunas opciones si no pueden pagar sus facturas. Por ejemplo, el año pasado ComEd inició un programa de descuentos para personas de bajos ingresos. Para más información, visita <a class="Link" href="http://www.comed.com/LID" target="_blank" >www.comed.com/LID</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/14/clientes-de-comed-podran-enfrentar-un-aumento-de-dos-digitos-en-sus-facturas-de-luz" target="_blank" >El Sun-Times informó el mes pasado</a> que los clientes de ComEd verán un aumento de al menos el 12% en los cargos mensuales a partir de junio, en parte debido a la demanda de energía creada por una explosión en la construcción de centros de datos de AI.</p><p>La <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/07/25/facturas-de-comed-se-mantendran-altas-porque-la-inteligencia-artificial-y-centros-de-datos-drenan-la-energia" target="_blank" >demanda por los centros de datos</a> no parece estar disminuyendo.</p><p>Quiniones indicó que hay aproximadamente 100 proyectos de centros de datos propuestos en el norte de Illinois, aunque es poco probable que todos avancen.</p><p>Los funcionarios de ComEd han dicho que comprenden que las facturas más altas representan otra carga financiera para las personas y los pequeños negocios. También se apresuran a explicar que la empresa de servicios públicos no produce energía. Más bien, los precios que ComEd paga por la electricidad están impulsados por la demanda futura prevista y fijados por el operador de la red eléctrica, PJM, con sede en Pensilvania.</p><p>“ComEd no establece, controla ni se beneficia de esos aumentos de precios”, ha afirmado la empresa.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: 22 alderpersons say they'll reject parking meters sale, accuse Johnson of holding back info about the deal
entries.summary: <p>At least 22 City Council members say they plan to reject the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/18/chicagos-parking-meters-could-be-sold-again-under-deal-requiring-city-council-approval" >sale of Chicago parking meters</a> to a New York investment firm, after accusing Mayor Brandon Johnson of withholding critical information from the Council and secretly agreeing to a June 30 deadline to authorize the transaction.</p><p></p><p>In a sharply worded letter to the mayor delivered Monday, the coalition of alderpersons said their decision to block the transfer of city parking meters from Chicago Parking Meters LLC to Stonepeak Partners is not based on the merits of the deal, but "on the fact that your administration has systematically withheld the information necessary for proper evaluation." </p><p>“Your administration agreed to a binding timeline on behalf of the City of Chicago without informing the body that must vote on the underlying transaction. This is not a procedural technicality. It is a fundamental failure of the separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches of city government,” the letter states.</p><p>In a statement released Monday, the Johnson administration maintained that the June 30 date is “not a deadline for Council action,” only the date by which the city must “report on Council’s progress.” The date does not change the City Council’s “independent authority over its review, determination or timeline for consideration” of the proposed meter transfer.</p><p>Johnson's office stated that the mayor introduced the ordinance authorizing the sale to Stonepeak “at the earliest practicable opportunity” after completing “procedural steps necessary to fulfill its obligations” in the concession agreement. “City Council remains an independent legislative body with sole authority to approve or reject the proposed transfer,” the statement said.</p><p> The letter was signed by many of the same Council members responsible for rejecting Johnson’s proposed corporate head tax before approving an alternative 2026 budget that includes replacement revenues opposed by the mayor. Stonepeak declined to comment on the Council members' letter.</p><p>Ald. Scott Waguespack (32nd) cast one of only five “no” votes against the lopsided parking meter deal that Chicagoans love to hate.</p><p>Waguespack said his decision to take a stand against the transfer to Stonepeak Partners has nothing to do with political grandstanding or holding out false hopes to change the "ironclad" deal that has already allowed private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi to nearly double their $1.15 billion outlay with 57 years to go on the original deal.</p><p>It’s about Johnson’s decision to agree to a June 30 deadline to approve the transfer to Stonepeak Partners without informing the legislative body that needs to take that pivotal vote. </p><p>“It was the administration that was making all the decisions. They ran out the clock on what should have been an information period for us of 60 days. And now they’re saying they have this deadline of June 30 and we have to sign off on it?” Waguespack told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“That’s so wholly unethical and lacks any concern for public accountability," he said. "It’s up to the mayor to find those votes. Yes, it could lead to arbitration or a lawsuit. But the mayor has put us in the position for that because of the lack of being open about this.”</p><p></p><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) added, "We're not a rubber stamp here. It's incumbent on all of us to understand what this deal is. ... There's not time for that. If there was actual collaboration going on, we would not be in this situation." </p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) said he and his colleagues will not be “forced into a corner to vote for something” by June 30 when the mayor’s office has had the information for months and chose to withhold it from the City Council.</p><p>“How can we make an educated decision when we’re not getting any of the information they were privvy to? To have your law department, your budget department and everybody in the mayor’s office say, 'Here’s the deal, but we can’t tell you anything about what’s in the deal' is total BS,” Beale said Monday. </p><p>Earlier this year, Johnson announced that City Hall had dropped out of the competition to take back Chicago parking meters after determining that the $3 billion asking price “would have made a bad deal even worse.”</p><p>The window opened last summer when Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi signaled their desire to unload Chicago parking meters and started inviting potential bids.</p><p>But after submitting an undisclosed bid, the mayor quickly learned that the asking price would have been nearly triple the $1.15 billion that Chicago received from the 75-year lease in 2008. Johnson decided that the risk wasn’t worth the reward, either financially or politically.</p><p>The letter to the mayor refers to that history and accuses Johnson of keeping the City Council in the dark every step of the way.</p><p>It claims that Johnson submitted a bid without informing — let alone seeking input from — the City Council, signed a nondisclosure agreement with Morgan Stanley without telling the Council until May 18, and waited until two weeks ago to inform Council members of the revised June 30 deadline to accept or reject the transfer to Stonepeak.</p><p>Even then, selected alderpersons were told the Finance and Law departments were “legally prohibited from sharing their analyses.”</p><p>“The Council has not received any accounting of criminal, civil or regulatory actions against Stonepeak or its affiliates, officers or directors, nor answers to basic questions about the ownership structure, the terms of the transfer, anticipated governance changes or whether the city faces any tax liability as a result of this transaction,” the letter states.</p><p>“They are the minimum threshold of information any legislative body would require before voting to approve a transfer of a public asset of this scale.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs release statement on moving Giants' Spanish broadcasters to press-box rafters
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs caused a stir in Northern California, and it had nothing to do with the action on the field this weekend.</p><p>After all, the Giants won the series and could've swept it.</p><p>The angst came from the Giants' Spanish-language radio crew being moved from a booth into the rafters of the Wrigley Field press box, according to John Shea of the San Francisco Standard. </p><p>On Friday, broadcasters Erwin Higueros and Carlos Orellana had the booth next to the Giants' English-speaking crew of Joe Ritzo and F.P. Santangelo.</p><p>But when ESPN Radio, an MLB rights holder, arrived for games Saturday and Sunday, the Cubs moved Higueros and Orellana to the upper reaches of the press box, which has an obstructed view. According to Shea, first and second base aren't visible, which isn't ideal for radio broadcasters. </p><p>After initially refusing comment Monday, the Cubs released this statement to the Sun-Times, from senior director of communications Jennifer Martinez<b>:</b></p><p>“The San Francisco Giants' Spanish-language radio broadcast team was provided a designated space in the Wrigley Field press box for all three games of the Giants vs. Cubs series. This space is regularly used whenever additional seating is needed. We look forward to hosting them again the next time the Giants are in town.”</p><p>There likely was little they could do to rectify the situation in the cramped space. For all the work done during the Wrigley Field renovation, the press box looks largely as it did when it opened in 1989. But declining to acknowledge that, or apologize for the inconvenience, casts the club in a bad light.</p><p>The Giants are among only four teams that have Spanish broadcasts for every game. The crew also travels for every road game. According to Shea, "sometimes they get a rude reminder of where they rank in MLB’s broadcast pecking order." </p><p>Shea wrote that neither Higueros nor Orellana complained, and they did the best they could. The crew also includes 82-year-old Tito Fuentes, who only works home games. The Giants always have had a strong following on Spanish radio.</p>
